deep.reconstruction:
This page contains no mathematics: no formulas, equations or derivations. It is a heavily revised, very faint pencil draft of the opening of Riemann's lecture course on partial differential equations and their application to physical questions. The course was first given in Göttingen in the mid-1850s and later edited by Hattendorff (1869). The previous page opens that introduction: 'Der Gegenstand dieser Vorlesungen ist die Behandlung der partiellen Differentialgleichungen ...'.

The page continues that methodological and historical argument.

(1) Upper left block (dense, faint): what seems to be the main point is roughly 'Wesentlich ... aber ist die Methode, durch welche man von den einfachen Grundgesetzen, welche für Zeitpunkte und Raumpunkte gelten, zu den Gesetzen für endliche Zeiten und Räume ... gelangt'. The thesis is that the decisive post-Newtonian progress lies in method, not in new basic concepts. That method is passing from elementary laws for infinitesimal time and space elements (differential equations) to integrated laws for finite intervals, which are the only ones observable. A mention of 'philosophischen' (probably the title of Newton's Principia, or a remark on natural philosophy) is visible mid-block.

(2) Right column, middle (partly legible): the differential equations express the law for a single time point and space point ('einfach als eines Zeitpunkts und Raumpunkts'). These must be integrated to obtain laws for extended regions.

(3) Lower half: a chronological sketch, with lines struck through and rewritten. The work cited appears to be Newton's 'Philosophiae naturalis principia mathematica' (visible fragment '... nat. princ. math.'), with a year read by the machine as 1637. Further dates read as 1727 and 1806.

(4) The next page continues with 'Jahre 1782', which is the classical date of Laplace's potential equation.

Overall this is the standard narrative (Galilei, then Newton, then the eighteenth-century creation of PDE theory by d'Alembert, Euler and Laplace, then Fourier) that also appears, in polished form, in the printed introduction to Riemann/Hattendorff. No computation is carried out, so there is nothing to reconstruct mathematically.
errors: No mathematical errors are possible since no mathematics is present. Historically, if the year read as '1637' is meant for Newton's Principia, the correct year is 1687. The faint digit is more likely 8 than 3; 1637 would instead be Descartes' Géométrie.
If '1806' refers to Fourier's heat memoir, the usual date is 1807 (submitted to the Académie, December 1807). The digit is uncertain.

results.what: Methodological thesis: physics since Newton has advanced not in its basic concepts (accelerating force, action at a distance) but in its method. That method is passing from elementary laws for infinitesimal space-time elements (differential equations) to integrated laws for finite domains.
results.modern_name: Philosophy of physics: the role of differential equations and the local-to-global integration of physical laws
results.usually_credited_to: Commonplace in 19th-century natural philosophy; Riemann's own formulation is printed in the introduction to Riemann/Hattendorff, 'Partielle Differentialgleichungen und deren Anwendung auf physikalische Fragen' (1869)

results.what: Historical chronology of the founding works (Newton's Principia, the 18th-century origins of PDEs, Laplace 1782, Fourier ca. 1807)
results.modern_name: History of mathematical physics / PDE theory

deep.surprise_reason: The page is a draft of the known, published introduction to Riemann's PDE lectures: methodological and historical prose with dates, with no mathematical content.
transcription_corrections: Top line: legible as roughly 'Wesentlich ... aber ist die Methode, durch welche man von den einfachen Grundgesetzen ...', continuing with 'für Zeitpunkte und Raumpunkte' and 'Gesetze für endliche ...' (Zeiten/Räume). This continues the previous page's argument.
The year read as '1637' is most likely '1687' (Newton's Principia). The right column of that line shows what looks like '... nat. princ. math.', i.e. 'Philosophiae naturalis principia mathematica'.
'1727' may be '1747' (d'Alembert's vibrating string equation), given the context of the origin of PDEs. The digit is uncertain.

Right column, middle block: fragments such as '... einfach als eines Zeitpunkts und Raumpunkts ...' and '... gestellte Differentialgleichungen ...' are partially legible. The machine transcription omits them.
The struck-through heading near the middle left ('Bild'?) is uncertain; it may be a cancelled word rather than a heading.
